paragraphs.heading: What a bond angle is
paragraphs.text: A bond angle is the angle made by three atoms linked across at least two bonds. It is one of the basic measurements of molecular geometry, the three-dimensional arrangement of a molecule's atoms. Along with bond lengths and torsional angles, bond angles help pin down where every atom sits.

paragraphs.heading: Its neighbours in geometry
paragraphs.text: A bond length is the average distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. A torsional angle needs a chain of four atoms: it is the angle between the plane through the first three and the plane through the last three. A bond angle, by contrast, involves three connected atoms.

paragraphs.heading: A local property
paragraphs.text: The angles between an atom's bonds are only weakly affected by the rest of the molecule. So they can be treated as roughly local properties, which also makes them transferable. Each atom's position is set by the kind of chemical bonds joining it to its neighbours.

paragraphs.heading: Angles around a central atom
paragraphs.text: Picture one central atom bonded to four outer atoms, which gives six bond angles to start with. These angles are not all free: a mathematical relationship, written as a determinant, ties them together. That constraint removes one degree of freedom, leaving only five angles that can be chosen.

paragraphs.heading: Where angles come from
paragraphs.text: Bond angles, like the rest of a molecule's geometry, come from the quantum mechanical behaviour of electrons. In the valence bond approximation, atomic orbitals combine as atoms bond, in a process called orbital hybridisation. Sigma bonds are usually formed from these hybrid orbitals, while pi bonds come from unhybridized p orbitals.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring them
paragraphs.text: NMR and FRET methods can supply angles and dihedral angles, along with relative distances and how atoms are connected. IR, microwave and Raman spectroscopy also reveal geometry through the way molecules vibrate and rotate. Such measurements are best made at low temperature, since warmer samples average over more shapes. Getting the shape right matters, because geometry affects a substance's reactivity, polarity, color and magnetism.
